title: Compare the main deployment strategies and their trade-offs (downtime, rollback speed, infra cost, risk) — Recreate, Rolling, Blue-Green (two environments, instant traffic switch + fast rollback), Canary (gradually shift a small % of traffic while watching metrics), A/B (compare experiences for a business metric), and Shadow (mirror prod traffic to the new version, discard its response); why is "zero downtime" an objective rather than a strategy, and how does expand-and-contract keep schema changes safe during rollout?
shortTitle: Comparing deployment strategies and their trade-offs — Recreate, Rolling, Blue-Green, Canary, A/B, Shadow

s1_definition.profdef: Deployment strategies are patterns for releasing a new version of a service, each trading off downtime, rollback speed, infrastructure cost, and risk differently. Recreate kills the old version then starts the new, accepting downtime. Rolling replaces pods incrementally for zero downtime with a slow rollback. Blue-Green runs two complete environments and flips a traffic switch for an instant cutover and instant rollback, at double the infrastructure cost. Canary shifts a small percentage of real traffic to the new version while watching metrics, expanding only if healthy. A/B routes users by an attribute to compare a business metric between two experiences. Shadow mirrors production traffic to the new version but discards its responses, so the new version is exercised under real load with zero user risk. Zero downtime is an objective because several of these strategies can achieve it, so it describes the goal, not the mechanism.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture National Bank of India opening a renovated counter. Recreate closes the old counter before opening the new one. Rolling swaps staff one at a time. Blue-Green builds a whole second counter and simply redirects the queue to it, keeping the old one ready in case of trouble. Canary sends every tenth customer to the new counter and watches if they are served well before sending more. A/B sends premium customers to one counter and regular customers to another to see which design closes more loans. Shadow quietly has the new counter process photocopies of real requests without giving the customer the result, just to see if it would cope. "Zero downtime" is the promise that the queue never stops — several of these counter plans can deliver it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Pick the strategy by how much you are willing to spend to shrink risk and rollback time — zero downtime is the destination, these strategies are different roads to it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Deployment strategies are patterns for releasing a new version of a service, each trading off downtime, rollback speed, infrastructure cost, and risk differently. Recreate kills the old version then starts the new, accepting downtime. Rolling replaces pods incrementally for zero downtime with a slow rollback. Blue-Green runs two complete environments and flips a traffic switch for an instant cutover and instant rollback, at double the infrastructure cost. Canary shifts a small percentage of real traffic to the new version while watching metrics, expanding only if healthy. A/B routes users by an attribute to compare a business metric between two experiences. Shadow mirrors production traffic to the new version but discards its responses, so the new version is exercised under real load with zero user risk. Zero downtime is an objective because several of these strategies can achieve it, so it describes the goal, not the mechanism.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture National Bank of India opening a renovated counter. Recreate closes the old counter before opening the new one. Rolling swaps staff one at a time. Blue-Green builds a whole second counter and simply redirects the queue to it, keeping the old one ready in case of trouble. Canary sends every tenth customer to the new counter and watches if they are served well before sending more. A/B sends premium customers to one counter and regular customers to another to see which design closes more loans. Shadow quietly has the new counter process photocopies of real requests without giving the customer the result, just to see if it would cope. "Zero downtime" is the promise that the queue never stops — several of these counter plans can deliver it.

**One line to remember:** Pick the strategy by how much you are willing to spend to shrink risk and rollback time — zero downtime is the destination, these strategies are different roads to it.

sections.s2_technical:
Recreate terminates all old instances and then starts the new ones. Its downtime is high because there is a gap with no running instances, its rollback is as slow as a full redeploy of the old version, its infrastructure cost is low because you never run extra instances, and its risk is high because all users hit the new version at once with no gradual exposure. It suits singletons and off-hours internal jobs.

Rolling replaces instances a few at a time. Its downtime is zero when readiness probes and graceful shutdown are correct, its rollback is slow because you must roll the old version back pod by pod, its cost is low to moderate because you only need room for the surge, and its risk is moderate because two versions coexist during the roll, so they must be compatible. It suits most stateless services.

Blue-Green runs two full environments, the current blue and the new green. You deploy and fully test green while blue serves all traffic, then flip the load balancer so all traffic goes to green instantly. Its downtime is effectively zero, its rollback is the fastest of all because you simply flip back to blue, its cost is high because you run two complete environments at once, and its risk is moderate: the cutover is all-or-nothing, so a bad green hits everyone the instant you switch, but you can revert in seconds. It suits releases where instant rollback matters more than gradual exposure.

Canary shifts a small slice of real traffic, perhaps five percent, to the new version while watching error rates, latency, and business metrics. If the canary stays healthy you expand to twenty-five, then fifty, then a hundred percent; if it degrades you abort and route everyone back to the old version. Its downtime is zero, its rollback is fast because only a small slice was ever exposed, its cost is moderate, and its risk is the lowest of the traffic-shifting strategies because problems are caught while affecting few users. It suits high-risk changes to critical paths.

A/B testing routes users by an attribute such as region, account tier, or a feature flag, to compare a business outcome between two experiences, for example which checkout flow produces more completed loan applications. It is a product-experiment technique that happens to use deployment routing. Its purpose is measuring a business metric, not primarily safety, though it shares the gradual-exposure benefit.

Shadow, also called traffic mirroring, sends a copy of real production requests to the new version while the old version still serves the user. The new version's responses are discarded and never reach the customer. This exercises the new code under genuine production load and data without any user-facing risk, which is invaluable for validating performance and correctness before any real cutover. Its user-facing downtime and risk are zero, but its cost is high because you run the new version in parallel and must carefully avoid side effects, since mirrored requests must not actually move money twice.

Zero downtime is an objective rather than a strategy because it names a property you want, not a mechanism. Rolling, Blue-Green, Canary, and Shadow can all deliver zero user-facing downtime, each by a different mechanism. Saying "we want zero downtime" does not tell you how; you still choose a strategy based on rollback speed, cost, and how gradually you want to expose the change.

The expand-and-contract pattern keeps schema changes safe during any rollout where two versions coexist. You split a breaking schema change into three steps. Expand: add the new structure, such as a new column, in a way that is backward compatible, so the old code ignores it and the new code can use it. Migrate: deploy the new code and backfill or dual-write data so both representations are populated. Contract: once no running code depends on the old structure, remove it. Because every intermediate state is readable and writable by whichever versions are live, a rolling update or canary never breaks, and a rollback never lands on a schema the old code cannot handle. In banking this is non-negotiable, because a half-applied destructive migration during a rollout could corrupt ledger data.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the platform team maintains a release playbook. Depending on the change, they pick a strategy, and they need a way to reason about the trade-offs consistently rather than arguing each time.

Problem 1 — A risky rewrite of the fraud-scoring path must go live, but if it misbehaves it could wrongly block Rajesh's legitimate transfers. The team cannot expose all customers at once. This is exactly the problem Canary solves: route a small percentage, watch the metrics, and expand only if healthy.

Problem 2 — A different release must be reversible in seconds because it touches the core transfer engine, and the business wants the ability to abort instantly for everyone. This is exactly the problem Blue-Green solves: keep the old environment hot and flip traffic back the moment anything looks wrong.

Problem 3 — Before any cutover, the team wants to validate that the new version can handle real production load and real data shapes without any customer seeing its output. This is exactly what Shadow does: mirror live requests, discard the responses, and compare behavior.

To make this runnable, we will build a small program that models traffic routing under each strategy. It will contain a `Version` enum for OLD and NEW, a `TrafficRouter` interface, and implementations for Rolling, Blue-Green, Canary, and Shadow that decide, for each incoming request, which version serves it and whether the response is used or discarded. A `ReleaseController` sends a stream of transfer requests through a chosen router and reports how traffic split and whether a rollback would be instant or gradual. The demo runs a canary at ten percent, a blue-green flip, and a shadow mirror, printing the routing decisions so the trade-offs are visible.

sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build and run the simulation
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/release-strategies-1.0.0.jar

# Real canary with a service mesh (Istio) — shift 10% then expand:
kubectl apply -f canary-virtualservice-10pct.yml
# watch metrics, then:
kubectl apply -f canary-virtualservice-50pct.yml
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a stream of one thousand transfer requests is routed under three strategies in turn — a canary at ten percent, a blue-green flip to the new environment, and a shadow mirror.

Step 1: The canary router runs. For each request it checks whether the request number modulo one hundred is below ten. About one hundred of the thousand requests are routed to the new version; the remaining nine hundred stay on the old version. The report shows roughly one hundred served by new, meaning only ten percent of customers are ever exposed while the team watches error and latency metrics.

Step 2: The canary's rollback description makes the trade-off explicit: because only ten percent were exposed, aborting is fast — route that slice back to the old version and no further customers are affected.

Step 3: The blue-green router starts with the old environment live, then the demo calls flip to make the new environment live. Now every one of the thousand requests is routed to the new version instantly. The report shows one thousand served by new. The rollback description notes this is instant: flipping the switch back sends everyone to the old environment in seconds.

Step 4: The shadow router runs. For every request, the user is served by the old version, and a copy is mirrored to the new version with the response discarded. The report shows zero served by new user-facing, but one thousand mirrored to new and thrown away. This means the new version was exercised under full production load with zero user risk.

Step 5: Comparing the three reports makes the trade-offs concrete. Canary exposed a small slice for real but gradual validation. Blue-green exposed everyone at once but can revert instantly. Shadow exposed no one yet still stress-tested the new version. Each achieved a different balance of risk, rollback speed, and cost.

Final output:

```text
Oct 25, 2026 1:40:02 AM com.bank.strategies.service.ReleaseController run
INFO: === Canary(10%) | rollback: fast — only 10% exposed, route them back to OLD ===
INFO: served by NEW (user-facing) = 100/1000
INFO: === Blue-Green(live=NEW) | rollback: instant — flip the switch back ===
INFO: served by NEW (user-facing) = 1000/1000
INFO: === Shadow | rollback: n/a — users never see NEW, zero user risk ===
INFO: served by NEW (user-facing) = 0/1000
INFO: mirrored to NEW (discarded) = 1000/1000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
There are six deployment strategies I reach for, and I compare them along four axes: downtime, rollback speed, infrastructure cost, and risk. Recreate kills the old version then starts the new, which means downtime but the lowest cost and no version overlap, so I use it for singletons and off-hours internal jobs. Rolling replaces instances incrementally for zero downtime at low cost, but rollback is slow because you unwind pod by pod, and two versions coexist during the roll so they must be compatible; it is my default for stateless services. Blue-Green runs two full environments and flips a load-balancer switch, giving an instant cutover and the fastest rollback of all, at the cost of running double the infrastructure; I use it when instant reversibility matters more than gradual exposure.

Canary shifts a small percentage of real traffic to the new version while I watch error rates, latency, and business metrics, then expands only if the canary stays healthy; it has the lowest risk of the traffic-shifting strategies because problems are caught while affecting few users, so I use it for high-risk changes to critical paths like fraud scoring. A/B testing routes users by an attribute such as account tier or region to compare a business outcome between two experiences; its purpose is measuring a business metric, not primarily safety. Shadow mirrors a copy of production traffic to the new version while the old version still serves the user and the new version's response is discarded, so the new code is exercised under real load and real data with zero user-facing risk, which is invaluable for validating performance before any cutover.

I always explain that zero downtime is an objective, not a strategy. It names a property I want, but several strategies — Rolling, Blue-Green, Canary, and Shadow — can each deliver it by a different mechanism. So saying the team wants zero downtime does not choose the approach; I still decide based on how fast I need to roll back, how much infrastructure I can afford, and how gradually I want to expose the change.

The piece I stress most for banking is expand-and-contract for schema changes, because any strategy where two versions run together will break if the database changes destructively mid-rollout. I split a breaking schema change into three steps. Expand: add the new structure, like a new column, in a backward-compatible way so old code ignores it and new code can use it. Migrate: deploy the new code and backfill or dual-write so both representations stay populated. Contract: only once no running code needs the old structure do I remove it. Because every intermediate state is readable and writable by whichever versions are live, a rolling update or canary never breaks and a rollback never lands on a schema the old code cannot handle. At National Bank of India, that discipline is what let us canary a fraud-scoring rewrite and keep blue-green ready for the core transfer engine without ever risking the ledger.

---

keyPoints: Rolling update: gradual replacement, zero downtime
Canary: small percentage first, then full rollout
Rollback: revert to previous version on failure
